summary: Specifies the Licklider Transmission Protocol, designed to give retransmission-based reliability over links with very long round-trip times or frequent interruptions, such as deep space links. It is aimed at long-haul reliable transmission and is published as an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: The Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP) is designed for links with very long delays or frequent interruptions. It can retransmit missing parts of a block while allowing other parts to be sent without acknowledgments.

questions: what is ltp licklider transmission protocol
what are red and green parts in ltp
subtitle: Selective retransmission for links with very long delays or frequent interruptions.

tldr.problem: Links with long round-trip times or frequent outages make ordinary retransmission-based protocols inefficient.
tldr.mechanism: Licklider Transmission Protocol (LTP) sends blocks in segments, marks a reliable red part, and uses reception reports and checkpoints to request missing data.
tldr.outcome: LTP is Experimental and has no flow-control or congestion-control mechanisms, so the RFC restricts where it should run.

today: RFC 5326 is Experimental. It states that LTP lacks flow and congestion control and is not intended for ubiquitous use on the global Internet.

sections.title: Reliability Across Disrupted Links
sections.content:
LTP is designed to provide retransmission-based reliability where messages take a long time to make a round trip or communication is interrupted often. Interplanetary communication is the main example described by the RFC.

LTP is stateful and uses selective acknowledgments, but it does not negotiate a connection with a handshake. In the described bundle-network setting, it can operate between adjacent nodes over a data-link protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: LTP is intended for links where waiting for a reply can take a long time or the link may disappear. It tracks the transfer and asks for reports about received data.

sections.title: Blocks, Segments, and Two Reliability Choices
sections.content:
An application gives LTP a block of data, which LTP sends as one or more segments. A block may have a red part that is acknowledged and retransmitted when needed, followed by a green part that is sent without acknowledgments or retransmissions.

Segments carry data, reception reports, report acknowledgments, or session-management messages. A checkpoint segment asks the receiver to report which data it has received, allowing the sender to identify missing ranges.
sections.plainLanguage: A block can mix a reliable red part with an unreliable green part. The receiver reports which red data arrived, and the sender retransmits the missing ranges.

sections.title: Reports and Retransmission
sections.content:
The sender starts a session and transmits segments. When it sends a checkpoint, the receiver returns a report describing received ranges within the report's scope; the sender acknowledges the report and retransmits data the report leaves unclaimed.

Timers support retransmission of checkpoints and reports when acknowledgments do not arrive. Either side can cancel a session, and the sender and receiver maintain state until completion or cancellation procedures close it.
sections.plainLanguage: A checkpoint prompts the receiver to report what arrived. The sender uses that report to resend missing data, and timers help recover when reports or acknowledgments are lost.

sections.title: Operating Environment and Security
sections.content:
The underlying protocol must meet requirements for transferring segments between LTP engines. If LTP runs over UDP, the RFC says it must be limited to software development or private local-area networks.

LTP provides no flow control or congestion control and is not intended for general deployment across the global Internet. The security section discusses denial-of-service and replay concerns and identifies implementation considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: LTP does not slow a sender to match network capacity. The RFC therefore limits UDP use to development or private local networks and does not recommend LTP for general Internet use.
